interpretations: Expensive means replacement_cost strictly greater than 20.99 (> 20.99). Average length per rating. Average of rental_rate / rental_duration per film per rating.
Expensive means replacement_cost greater than or equal to 20.99 (>= 20.99). Average length per rating. Average of rental_rate / rental_duration per film per rating.
The per-film average of rental_rate / rental_duration is computed as the mean of each film's ratio (AVG(rental_rate / rental_duration)). This is what the question literally describes.
The per-film average of rental_rate / rental_duration is computed as a ratio of averages (AVG(rental_rate) / AVG(rental_duration)).
The per-film average of rental_rate / rental_duration is computed as a ratio of sums (SUM(rental_rate) / SUM(rental_duration)).
Averages are taken over film rows in the film table, with one row per film. Films are not weighted by the number of inventory copies.
Averages are weighted by inventory copies, by joining film to inventory. Films with no copies are dropped, and films with more copies count more.
Only films that have at least one inventory copy are counted as expensive films, but each film is counted once.
Result rows are limited to ratings that have at least one expensive film. Ratings with no expensive films are omitted.
All five ratings are listed, and ratings with no expensive films show NULL averages.
Average length ignores NULL lengths in the usual way (AVG(length)). The per-film ratio average ignores NULL ratios the same way.
Films with a NULL length are excluded entirely from the group, so the ratio average is also computed only over films that have a length.
The filter on replacement_cost is applied before grouping (WHERE), so only the expensive films enter the averages.
The cutoff is applied per group after aggregation (HAVING), such as keeping ratings whose average replacement_cost exceeds 20.99.
The output has three columns: rating, average length, and average rental_rate / rental_duration, with no rounding or formatting.
The rental_rate / rental_duration ratio is computed with integer division, which truncates the result.
The rental_rate / rental_duration ratio is computed with exact decimal or floating-point division, giving a fractional value per day.
The rating groups are ordered in the output by rating name, by rating severity (G, PG, PG-13, R, NC-17), or in no particular order.
Missing interpretations:

Expensive films are those with replacement_cost at or above 20.99, rounded to the nearest cent. This is the same as >= 20.99, but it accounts for floating-point or decimal representation of the cutoff.
The per-film ratio average is computed only over films that have a non-NULL rental_duration and rental_rate. Zero or NULL rental_duration is excluded to avoid division by zero.
"Per film" means the average is taken over distinct films, so duplicate film rows are collapsed. This matters if film_text or other joins create duplicates.

The ratio average is computed as the average of per-film values after the length average has been calculated separately. Each aggregate then uses its own set of non-NULL rows. Films with a NULL length still count toward the ratio average.
Average length is computed after converting length to a decimal or float type, so no integer truncation occurs.
Ratings are grouped case-insensitively or after trimming whitespace, so variants such as 'pg-13' and 'PG-13' fall into one group.
Films with a NULL rating form their own group, or they are dropped.
queries:
SELECT rating, AVG(length), AVG(rental_rate / rental_duration)
FROM film
WHERE replacement_cost > 20.99
GROUP BY rating;
SELECT rating, AVG(length), AVG(rental_rate / rental_duration) FROM film WHERE replacement_cost >= 20.99 GROUP BY rating
